cards.question: What is the primary definition of a data structure?
cards.answer: A specialized format for organizing, managing, and storing data in computer memory to enable efficient access and modification.

cards.question: What is an Abstract Data Type (ADT)?
cards.answer: A mathematical model of data objects defined solely by their behavior and supported operations, independent of any specific implementation.

cards.question: What are the five essential characteristics of an algorithm?
cards.answer: Input (zero or more), Output (at least one), Definiteness (unambiguous steps), Finiteness (terminates in finite steps), and Effectiveness (feasible operations).

cards.question: How do linear data structures differ from non-linear data structures?
cards.answer: Linear structures (arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues) arrange elements sequentially; non-linear structures (trees, graphs) arrange elements hierarchically or interconnectedly.

cards.question: What is the difference between static and dynamic data structures?
cards.answer: Static structures have a fixed size allocated at compile time (like standard arrays), whereas dynamic structures grow or shrink during runtime (like linked lists).

cards.question: What is the difference between Time Complexity and Space Complexity?
cards.answer: Time complexity quantifies the amount of time/operations an algorithm takes as a function of input size; space complexity quantifies the auxiliary memory consumed.

cards.question: What does Big-O notation (O) represent in algorithmic analysis?
cards.answer: An asymptotic upper bound that describes the worst-case growth rate of an algorithm's resource consumption as input size approaches infinity.

cards.question: What does Big-Omega (Ω) notation represent?
cards.answer: An asymptotic lower bound that describes the minimum growth rate or best-case lower limit of an algorithm's execution time.

cards.question: What does Big-Theta (Θ) notation represent?
cards.answer: An asymptotically tight bound where an algorithm's upper and lower bounds share the same growth rate within constant factors.

cards.question: What is the standard hierarchy of algorithmic complexity growth rates?
cards.answer: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(n^3) < O(2^n) < O(n!), ordered from most efficient to least efficient.

cards.question: How does Linear Search work and what is its time complexity?
cards.answer: It sequentially checks every element from start to finish. Best-case is O(1) (found at index 0); worst-case is O(n) (not found or at end).

cards.question: How does Binary Search achieve O(log n) efficiency?
cards.answer: On a sorted array, it compares the target with the middle element and discards half the search space in each step, taking at most ceil(log2 n) comparisons.

cards.question: How does Bubble Sort operate?
cards.answer: It repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if out of order, bubbling the largest unsorted element to the end (O(n^2) time).

cards.question: What is the core mechanism of Selection Sort?
cards.answer: It repeatedly finds the minimum element from the unsorted section and swaps it with the first element of that unsorted section (O(n^2) comparisons always).

cards.question: How does Insertion Sort work and when is it fastest?
cards.answer: It builds the sorted array by inserting each unsorted element into its proper position among sorted items; best-case is O(n) on an already-sorted array.

cards.question: What is the Divide-and-Conquer strategy in sorting?
cards.answer: A strategy that divides a problem into smaller subproblems, solves the subproblems recursively, and combines their solutions (used in Merge Sort and Quick Sort).

cards.question: What are the time and space complexities of Merge Sort?
cards.answer: Time complexity is O(n log n) in all cases (best, average, worst); auxiliary space complexity is O(n) for the temporary merge buffer.

cards.question: How does Quick Sort partition an array?
cards.answer: It selects a pivot element and rearranges elements so that values <= pivot are placed left and values > pivot are right, placing the pivot in its final sorted index.

cards.question: When does Quick Sort exhibit its worst-case O(n^2) behavior?
cards.answer: When the chosen pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element (such as choosing the first element on an already-sorted array).

cards.question: What is stability in sorting algorithms?
cards.answer: A sorting algorithm is stable if it preserves the relative original order of records that have equal key values (e.g., Merge Sort and Insertion Sort are stable).

cards.question: What are the primary trade-offs between Arrays and Linked Lists?
cards.answer: Arrays offer O(1) random indexing but fixed size and O(n) insertion/deletion shifting; Linked Lists offer dynamic size and O(1) insertion at known pointers, but O(n) access.

cards.question: What are the components of a Singly Linked List Node?
cards.answer: A data field (data or info) storing the element value and a pointer field (next) storing the memory address of the next node.

cards.question: What is the role of the head pointer and how does a singly linked list terminate?
cards.answer: The head pointer stores the address of the first node (or NULL if empty); the next pointer of the last node is set to NULL.

cards.question: How is a new node inserted at the beginning of a Singly Linked List in O(1) time?
cards.answer: newNode->next = head; head = newNode; — first connect the new node to current first node, then update head to point to newNode.

cards.question: How is the first node deleted from a Singly Linked List in O(1) time?
cards.answer: Node *temp = head; head = head->next; delete temp; — save head in a temporary pointer, advance head, and free the old node.

cards.question: What is the node structure of a Doubly Linked List?
cards.answer: Each node contains three fields: prev (pointer to previous node), data (information payload), and next (pointer to next node).

cards.question: What are the main benefits of a Doubly Linked List over a Singly Linked List?
cards.answer: Bidirectional traversal (forward and backward) and easier deletion of a given node in O(1) without needing to traverse from head to find the predecessor.

cards.question: What characterizes a Circular Linked List?
cards.answer: The last node's next pointer points back to the first node (head) instead of NULL, creating a continuous circular loop.

cards.question: What is a Skip List?
cards.answer: A multi-level linked list with probabilistic forward pointers that allow skipping multiple nodes to achieve O(log n) average search, insertion, and deletion.

cards.question: What are Self-Organizing Lists and Unrolled Linked Lists?
cards.answer: Self-organizing lists reorder nodes based on access frequency (e.g. Move-to-Front); unrolled linked lists store arrays of items per node for better cache performance.

cards.question: What is a Stack and what is its governing principle?
cards.answer: A linear data structure operating under the LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) principle, where all additions and removals occur exclusively at the top.

cards.question: What are the primary operations of a Stack?
cards.answer: push(x) (adds an item onto top), pop() (removes and returns topmost item), top()/peek() (inspects top item), isEmpty(), and isFull().

cards.question: Why are infix expressions converted to postfix notation for machines?
cards.answer: Infix expressions require operator precedence and parentheses rules that complicate parsing; postfix expressions can be evaluated linearly in a single pass using a stack.

cards.question: How does a Stack evaluate a Postfix expression?
cards.answer: Scan left-to-right: push operands onto stack; when an operator is encountered, pop top two operands, apply operator, and push result back.

cards.question: What is a Queue and what is its governing principle?
cards.answer: A linear data structure operating under the FIFO (First-In-First-Out) principle, where insertions occur at the rear and deletions occur at the front.

cards.question: How does a Circular Queue eliminate wasted space?
cards.answer: It wraps front and rear indices around the ends of the array using modulo arithmetic: rear = (rear + 1) % size and front = (front + 1) % size.

cards.question: What is a Deque and a Priority Queue?
cards.answer: A Deque allows insertion/deletion at both ends (O(1)); a Priority Queue serves elements according to assigned priority rather than arrival sequence.

cards.question: What are the two essential components of any recursive function?
cards.answer: A Base Case (stopping condition that returns directly without further recursion) and a General/Recursive Case (reduces problem toward the base case).

cards.question: What is the Three-Question Method for verifying recursion?
cards.answer: Base-Case Question (is there a non-recursive exit?), Smaller-Caller Question (does each call work on a smaller problem?), and General-Case Question (is the result correct?).

cards.question: How does the Call Stack manage recursive executions?
cards.answer: Each recursive call pushes an Activation Record (local variables, parameters, return address) onto the Call Stack and pops it when the call completes.

cards.question: What are Root, Leaf, and Height in tree terminology?
cards.answer: Root is the top node with no parent; Leaf is a node with degree 0 (no children); Height is the length of the longest path from root to any leaf node.

cards.question: What are Full, Complete, and Perfect Binary Trees?
cards.answer: Full: all nodes have 0 or 2 children; Complete: all levels full except possibly last (filled left-to-right); Perfect: all internal nodes have 2 children and leaves are at same level.

cards.question: How is a Binary Tree represented sequentially in an array?
cards.answer: For 0-indexed root: a node at index i has its left child at 2i + 1, right child at 2i + 2, and parent at floor((i - 1) / 2).

cards.question: What is the Binary Search Tree (BST) property?
cards.answer: For every node X, all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller than X's key, and all keys in the right subtree are strictly greater than X's key.

cards.question: How is a node with two children deleted from a BST?
cards.answer: Replace the node's value with its Inorder Successor (minimum of right subtree) or Inorder Predecessor, then delete that successor/predecessor node.

cards.question: What are Preorder, Inorder, and Postorder Traversals?
cards.answer: Preorder is Node-Left-Right (NLR); Inorder is Left-Node-Right (LNR, produces sorted keys in BST); Postorder is Left-Right-Node (LRN).

cards.question: How is Level-Order Traversal implemented?
cards.answer: Using a FIFO Queue to visit nodes level by level from left to right (enqueue root, then repeatedly dequeue node and enqueue its left and right children).

cards.question: How does the DSW Algorithm rebalance a BST?
cards.answer: Phase 1 creates a backbone (right-skewed vine) via right rotations in O(n) time; Phase 2 performs left rotations using M = 2^(floor(log2(n+1))) - 1 to build a balanced tree in O(n) time.

cards.question: What is an AVL Tree and how is Balance Factor defined?
cards.answer: A self-balancing BST where the balance factor BF = height(Left) - height(Right) in {-1, 0, +1} for every node, guaranteeing O(log n) operations.

cards.question: What are the four types of AVL Tree rotations?
cards.answer: Single Left (RR), Single Right (LL), Left-Right (LR: left on child then right on parent), and Right-Left (RL: right on child then left on parent).
